**Case Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 68-year-old married man, a career politician who served for decades as a city councilman and later as a state senator. He presents for evaluation at the urging of his wife, who has grown concerned about his withdrawal and irritability over the past eight months.

The traumatic event occurred on a clear Tuesday afternoon, eight months ago. Mr. A. was driving his sedan on a rural two-lane highway, returning from a constituent meeting. He recalls a flash of sunlight on chrome, then a deafening impact. A pickup truck, driven by a teenager on his phone, had crossed the center line. Mr. A.’s car was T-boned, rolled twice, and came to rest upside down in a drainage ditch. He was trapped for forty-five minutes, suspended by his seatbelt, the smell of gasoline and hot metal flooding the cabin. He remembers the sound of his own breathing, the distant siren, and the thought, clear as a bell: *This is it. I’m going to die here. My work is unfinished.* He sustained a fractured clavicle, three broken ribs, and a concussion. The teenager walked away with bruises.

Physically, Mr. A. has healed. He returned to the state capitol after six weeks of convalescence. But the man who returned is not the man who left. His staff, once accustomed to his booming laugh and relentless energy, now finds him short-tempered and distracted. He cancels meetings without explanation. He has stopped taking the back roads to his district office, insisting on the interstate, even though it adds twenty minutes to his commute. He cannot explain why, except to say, “I just don’t like those roads anymore.”

At home, his wife describes him as a “ghost.” He sits in his study for hours, staring at his computer screen, unable to write a simple speech. The words are there, but they feel hollow. He has stopped attending the weekly poker game he’d hosted for thirty years. When she asks why, he snaps, “What’s the point? It’s all just noise.”

He experiences the intrusion of the accident with a vividness that shames him. Two nights ago, while watching a news report about a highway pileup, he felt his heart pound so hard he thought he was having a heart attack. He broke into a cold sweat, his hands trembled, and he had to leave the room. He now checks the rearview mirror obsessively while driving, sometimes ten times a minute. He avoids driving altogether after dark. The sound of a car horn—even a polite tap—makes him flinch and curse under his breath.

His sleep is a battleground. He wakes at 3:00 AM, drenched, the smell of gasoline in his nostrils. In the dream, he is always upside down, the steering wheel crushing his chest, and he cannot scream. He has begun drinking two glasses of whiskey before bed to “take the edge off,” and his wife has found him asleep in the armchair in his study, as if he is afraid to lie down in the dark.

The most painful change is in his sense of purpose. He used to believe in the slow, grinding work of legislation—the handshakes, the compromises, the small victories. Now, he tells me it all feels like “stagecraft.” He looks at the young aides buzzing around the capitol and feels a profound, cold distance. “They’re all so serious,” he says, with a bitter laugh. “They don’t know. In a second, it’s all gone. The votes, the bills, the photo ops. It’s just a car in a ditch.”

He is not suicidal, but he has stopped planning for the future. He used to have a five-year plan for his final term. Now, he cannot imagine next month. He tells his wife he’s “just tired,” but the fatigue is not physical. It is a deep, existential exhaustion, the weight of a man who looked into the abyss and found that all his speeches were just words.
